name: Volume-conditioned index autocorrelation: reverse high-volume moves, extend low-volume moves, 13 equity ETFs (Campbell-Grossman-Wang)
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Needs i>=21. r=ret(i). vbar=mean of volume over bars i-20..i-1 (the prior 20 sessions, today excluded; ctx.rollingMean('volume',20,i-1)). If vbar<=0 or |r|<0.005 return 0. q=volume[i]/vbar. If q>1 return -sign(r) (a high-volume move is liquidity-driven and expected to reverse); else return +sign(r) (a low-volume move is information-driven and expected to continue). Hold one bar, re-decided every bar.
rationale: Campbell, Grossman and Wang show first-order return autocorrelation turns more negative on high-volume days because liquidity demand moves prices that then revert, while low-volume moves carry information and persist. The rule tests that sign flip on index and sector ETFs.
source: Campbell, Grossman & Wang 1993, 'Trading volume and serial correlation in stock returns', Quarterly Journal of Economics 108(4), 905-939

name: Volatility-conditioned index autocorrelation: continue moves in calm regimes, reverse them in turbulent regimes, 13 equity ETFs (Sentana-Wadhwani)
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Needs i>=253. r=ret(i). s21=ctx.rollingStd('ret',21,i), s252=ctx.rollingStd('ret',252,i). If |r|<0.005 return 0. If s21<s252 (calm regime) return +sign(r); otherwise (turbulent regime) return -sign(r). Hold one bar, re-decided every bar.
rationale: Sentana and Wadhwani show feedback traders make daily index returns positively autocorrelated when volatility is low and negatively autocorrelated when it is high. The rule trades that state-dependent sign.
source: Sentana & Wadhwani 1992, 'Feedback traders and stock return autocorrelations: evidence from a century of daily data', Economic Journal 102(411), 415-425; LeBaron 1992, Economics Letters 40(1), 71-75

name: Volume-conditioned hourly autocorrelation in crypto: fade high-volume 1.5-sigma hours, follow low-volume ones (Campbell-Grossman-Wang transfer)
rule: signal() mode on hourly bars, per asset; bars[0..i] only; the value at bar i is held over bar i+1. Needs i>=169. r=ret(i)=close[i]/close[i-1]-1 (hourly). sig=ctx.rollingStd('ret',168,i). vbar=ctx.rollingMean('volume',24,i-1) (prior 24 hours, current hour excluded). If vbar<=0 or |r|<1.5*sig return 0. q=volume[i]/vbar. If q>1 return -sign(r); else return +sign(r).
rationale: Intraday liquidity provision should make large high-volume hourly moves revert and large low-volume moves continue, the same mechanism Campbell, Grossman and Wang document daily. Crypto trades continuously with fragmented liquidity, so the test is whether it survives 0.10% per side costs.
source: Campbell, Grossman & Wang 1993, QJE 108(4), 905-939 (applied to hourly crypto bars)

name: Brock-Lakonishok-LeBaron fixed-length rule: 10-day hold after a 1% penetration of the 50-day average, 13 equity ETFs
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Fixed-length-holding variant (FMA). meta.holdBars=10: the harness holds a non-zero signal for exactly 10 bars and ignores signals while a trade is open. Needs i>=51. s=ctx.sma('close',50,i), sp=ctx.sma('close',50,i-1). Return 1 iff close[i]>1.01*s AND close[i-1]<=1.01*sp (a fresh upward penetration of the 1% band); otherwise 0. Sell signals are not traded (long-only, flat otherwise).
rationale: BLL's strongest result was the buy-signal returns over a fixed ten days after a band-filtered crossing, not a hold-until-reversal rule. This tests that fixed-holding design, which differs from the always-in-the-market 200-day rules already run.
source: Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron 1992, 'Simple technical trading rules and the stochastic properties of stock returns', Journal of Finance 47(5), 1731-1764

name: Brock-Lakonishok-LeBaron trading-range break on crypto: close 1% above the 50-day closing high, exit 1% below the 50-day closing low
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Needs i>=51. R=max(close[i-50..i-1]) and Sp=min(close[i-50..i-1]) (prior 50 closes, today excluded). State ctx.state.pos (init 0 via the undefined check). If pos==0 and close[i]>1.01*R then pos=1. Else if pos==1 and close[i]<0.99*Sp then pos=0. Return pos. Long-only.
rationale: The trading-range break (resistance/support) rule is the second family in Brock et al. and was tested on Bitcoin by Gerritsen et al., who found it among the more consistent technical rules. This runs it across 18 coins with the original 1% band.
source: Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron 1992, Journal of Finance 47(5), 1731-1764; Gerritsen, Bouri, Ramezanifar & Roubaud 2020, 'The profitability of technical trading rules in the Bitcoin market', Finance Research Letters 34, 101263

name: Volume-augmented moving average rule: close above the 50-day average while 10-day volume exceeds 50-day volume, 13 equity ETFs
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Needs i>=51. Return 1 iff close[i]>ctx.sma('close',50,i) AND ctx.sma('volume',10,i)>ctx.sma('volume',50,i); otherwise 0. Long-only, re-decided every bar.
rationale: Blume, Easley and O'Hara argue volume reveals the quality of price information, and Gencay and Stengos found adding volume-average ratios to moving-average rules improved forecasts. This tests the plain volume-gated rule against price-only trend rules.
source: Blume, Easley & O'Hara 1994, 'Market statistics and technical analysis: the role of volume', Journal of Finance 49(1), 153-181; Gencay & Stengos 1998, Journal of Forecasting 17(5-6), 401-414

name: Alexander filter rule at 8%: buy after an 8% rise from the trough, sell after an 8% fall from the peak, 25 ETFs
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Needs i>=1. State ctx.state: pos (0 flat / 1 long), ext. At the first bar seen (ext undefined): pos=0, ext=close[i] (trough). Each bar: if pos==0 then ext=min(ext,close[i]) and, if close[i]>=ext*(1+0.08), pos=1 and ext=close[i] (peak). Else (pos==1) ext=max(ext,close[i]) and, if close[i]<=ext*(1-0.08), pos=0 and ext=close[i] (trough). Return pos. Long-only.
rationale: Alexander's x% filter rule and Fama and Blume's test of it is the original trend-following benchmark: it was profitable before costs for small x and not after costs. This tests one mid-size filter across the full 25-ETF discovery set with modern costs.
source: Alexander 1961, 'Price movements in speculative markets: trends or random walks', Industrial Management Review 2(2), 7-26; Fama & Blume 1966, 'Filter rules and stock-market trading', Journal of Business 39(1), 226-241

name: Alexander filter rule at 20% on crypto: buy after a 20% rise from the trough, sell after a 20% fall from the peak, 18 coins
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Needs i>=1. State ctx.state: pos (0/1), ext. At the first bar seen (ext undefined): pos=0, ext=close[i]. Each bar: if pos==0 then ext=min(ext,close[i]) and, if close[i]>=ext*1.20, pos=1 and ext=close[i]. Else ext=max(ext,close[i]) and, if close[i]<=ext*0.80, pos=0 and ext=close[i]. Return pos. Long-only.
rationale: Crypto moves are several times larger than equity moves, so the filter threshold is scaled up; filter rules are the most-cited simple technical test on Bitcoin. It is the same published rule as the ETF version on a different asset class and scale.
source: Alexander 1961, Industrial Management Review 2(2), 7-26; Fama & Blume 1966, Journal of Business 39(1), 226-241

name: Nearness to the 52-week high predicts the index: hold QQQ/DIA only when within 5% of the 252-day closing high (Li-Yu)
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Needs i>=251. H=max(close[i-251..i]) (252 closes including today). N=close[i]/H. Return 1 iff N>=0.95; otherwise 0. Long-only, re-decided every bar.
rationale: Li and Yu find that nearness of the Dow to its 52-week high positively predicts aggregate market returns because investors anchor on it and underreact to good news. The time-series index version differs from the cross-sectional 52-week-high stock and sector rules already run.
source: Li & Yu 2012, 'Investor attention, psychological anchors, and stock return predictability', Journal of Financial Economics 104(2), 401-419

name: Large one-day decline reversal: buy after a close-to-close drop of 7% or more, hold 5 sessions (Cox-Peterson)
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Wide-universe signal mode: set meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_WIDE' and do not also set meta.assets. meta.holdBars=5 (a non-zero signal opens a trade held exactly 5 bars; signals during an open trade are ignored). Return 1 iff ret(i)<=-0.07; otherwise 0. Long-only.
rationale: Cox and Peterson find large one-day declines are followed by short-term reversals that fade or vanish in more liquid, recent samples. The test asks whether the reversal still exists in liquid large caps after costs.
source: Cox & Peterson 1994, 'Stock returns following large one-day declines: evidence on short-term reversals and longer-term performance', Journal of Finance 49(1), 255-267

name: Fade large no-news moves: short or buy 5%+ one-day moves that came on under 1.5x normal volume, hold 10 sessions (Chan)
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Wide-universe signal mode: set meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_WIDE' and do not also set meta.assets. meta.holdBars=10. Needs i>=21. r=ret(i). vbar=mean of volume over bars i-20..i-1. q=volume[i]/vbar (return 0 if vbar<=0). If |r|>=0.05 AND q<1.5 return -sign(r) (fade the move); otherwise 0. longShort true. Volume is the a priori proxy for 'no news': news-driven moves come on heavy volume and are excluded.
rationale: Chan finds stocks with big moves and no headlines reverse, while moves with news drift on. Without a news feed, quiet volume is the only no-news proxy, so this tests the reversal half on large caps.
source: Chan 2003, 'Stock price reaction to news and no-news: drift and reversal after headlines', Journal of Financial Economics 70(2), 223-260

name: Friday-to-Monday persistence: take Monday in the direction of Friday's return, 13 equity ETFs (Cross; Abraham-Ikenberry)
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Needs i>=1. If dow(bars[i].time)==5 (Friday) and ret(i)>0 return 1; if dow==5 and ret(i)<0 return -1; on every other day return 0. The position is held over bar i+1, normally the following Monday session. longShort true.
rationale: Cross found that when Friday closes up Monday tends to be up, and Abraham and Ikenberry tie weak Mondays to selling by individual investors after down Fridays. This tests the conditional weekend rule on liquid ETFs; the unconditional Monday effect is already in the registry.
source: Cross 1973, 'The behavior of stock prices on Fridays and Mondays', Financial Analysts Journal 29(6), 67-69; Abraham & Ikenberry 1994, 'The individual investor and the weekend effect', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 29(2), 263-277

name: Lottery-avoidance composite: long the least lottery-like fifth by MAX, idiosyncratic volatility and idiosyncratic skewness (Kumar; Bali-Cakici-Whitelaw)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta: universe 'US_STOCKS_WIDE' (do not also set meta.assets). Monthly rebalance. Eligible if L>=64. EW market r_m(k)=equal-weight mean of ret(b,k) over every eligible name with bar k, for k=e-62..e (built from universe bars up to e). For each name: OLS of ret(b,k) on r_m(k) over k=e-62..e (63 obs), residuals u_k; ivol=sample std of u; iskew=mean((u-mean(u))^3)/(population std of u)^3; MAX=max of ret(b,k) over k=e-20..e. Percentile-rank each of the three across eligible names (0 lowest .. 1 highest value); composite=(P_MAX+P_ivol+P_iskew)/3. Long the lowest 20% (round down) by composite, equal weight; fewer than 3 picks -> {}. Kumar's nominal-price leg is dropped because the cached bars are split-adjusted. Percentile rank P of a name = (its zero-based position when the eligible names are sorted ascending by that value, ties by symbol name ascending) / (N-1), N = number of eligible names.
rationale: Kumar shows lottery-like stocks (high idiosyncratic volatility and skewness) are overpriced because retail investors gamble on them. Each ingredient has been run alone; this tests the combined lottery score as an avoidance screen.
source: Kumar 2009, 'Who gambles in the stock market?', Journal of Finance 64(4), 1889-1933; Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw 2011, 'Maxing out: stocks as lotteries and the cross-section of expected returns', Journal of Financial Economics 99(2), 427-446
prereg_note: clarified percentile-rank definition at prereg time; no parameter change

name: Merton idiosyncratic-risk premium: long the highest-idiosyncratic-volatility fifth, monthly (Merton; Fu)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta: universe 'US_STOCKS_WIDE' (do not also set meta.assets). Monthly rebalance. Eligible if L>=64. r_m(k)=EW mean of ret(b,k) over eligible names with bar k, k=e-62..e. ivol_s=sample std of the residuals of OLS ret(b,k) on r_m(k) over those 63 bars. Long the top 20% (round down) by ivol, equal weight; fewer than 3 picks -> {}.
rationale: Merton's incomplete-information model says under-diversified investors demand compensation for idiosyncratic risk, and Fu finds a positive premium when volatility is forecast; Ang et al. find the opposite. The registry only holds the low-idiosyncratic-volatility sign, so this is the other published sign.
source: Merton 1987, 'A simple model of capital market equilibrium with incomplete information', Journal of Finance 42(3), 483-510; Fu 2009, 'Idiosyncratic risk and the cross-section of expected stock returns', Journal of Financial Economics 91(1), 24-37

name: Crypto value-at-risk premium: long the 6 coins with the largest 5% daily-loss size over 90 days, weekly (Bali-Cakici transfer)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta: universe 'CRYPTO_DAILY', weekly rebalance. Eligible if L>=92. Take ret(b,k) for k=e-89..e (90 obs) sorted ascending as x[0..89]; VaR_s=-x[4] (the 5th smallest return, 5% empirical quantile, zero-based index 4). Long the 6 highest VaR_s, 1/6 each.
rationale: Bali and Cakici find stocks with larger value-at-risk earn higher subsequent returns, a tail-risk premium separate from volatility. Crypto has the fattest tails of any liquid asset, so it is the natural transfer.
source: Bali & Cakici 2004, 'Value at risk and expected stock returns', Financial Analysts Journal 60(2), 57-73

name: Crypto nominal-price effect: long the 6 lowest-priced coins, weekly (Liu-Tsyvinski-Wu price factors; Birru-Wang)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta: universe 'CRYPTO_DAILY', weekly rebalance. Eligible if L>=2. price_s=b[e].close in USDT. Long the 6 lowest price_s, 1/6 each. Coin prices are not split-adjusted, so nominal price is a real quantity here.
rationale: Liu, Tsyvinski and Wu find low-priced coins earn higher returns in their size factors, and Birru and Wang show investors treat nominal price as a signal of cheapness and skewness. The rule is the plain price-level sort.
source: Liu, Tsyvinski & Wu 2022, 'Common risk factors in cryptocurrency', Journal of Finance 77(2), 1133-1177; Birru & Wang 2016, 'Nominal price illusion', Journal of Financial Economics 119(3), 578-598

name: Unlevered risk parity across 7 asset-class ETFs: inverse 1-year volatility weights, monthly (Asness-Frazzini-Pedersen)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta.assets=the 7 ETFs, monthly rebalance. Eligible if L>=253. sigma_s=sample std of ret(b,k) over k=e-251..e. If fewer than 4 eligible return {}. w_s=(1/sigma_s)/sum over eligible of (1/sigma). Weights sum to 1; no leverage.
rationale: Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen argue leverage-averse investors overpay for risky assets, so equalising risk contributions across asset classes earns a higher Sharpe than market weights. The unlevered version is the retail 'All Weather' shape; the harness benchmark is equal weight.
source: Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen 2012, 'Leverage aversion and risk parity', Financial Analysts Journal 68(1), 47-59

name: Size effect via dollar volume: long the smallest fifth by 63-day dollar volume, monthly (Banz)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta: universe 'US_STOCKS_WIDE' (do not also set meta.assets). Monthly rebalance. Eligible if L>=64. DV_s=mean over k=e-62..e of b[k].close*b[k].volume. Long the lowest 20% (round down) by DV_s, equal weight; fewer than 3 picks -> {}. Dollar volume is the size proxy because market capitalisation is not cached.
rationale: Banz documents that smaller firms earn higher risk-adjusted returns; dollar volume is a standard price-volume proxy for size. Inside a large-cap-heavy universe the smallest fifth are the least-traded mid caps.
source: Banz 1981, 'The relationship between return and market value of common stocks', Journal of Financial Economics 9(1), 3-18

name: Mutual-fund October tax year-end: buy stocks down 20% or more over the prior 250 sessions at the first close on or after Oct 28, hold 8 sessions (Gibson-Safieddine-Titman)
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Wide-universe signal mode: set meta.universe 'US_STOCKS_WIDE' and do not also set meta.assets. meta.holdBars=8. Needs i>=250. Entry bar: ymd(i)>=(Y,10,28) and ymd(i-1)<(Y,10,28) for some year Y. At the entry bar return 1 iff close[i]/close[i-250]-1<=-0.20; otherwise 0. The harness holds the trade 8 bars (to about Nov 7). On every other bar return 0. Long-only.
rationale: Gibson, Safieddine and Titman find funds with an October fiscal year-end sell losers before the tax deadline, depressing prices that rebound in early November. This tests the rebound on liquid large caps, separately from the December tax-loss window.
source: Gibson, Safieddine & Titman 2000, 'Tax-motivated trading and price pressure: an analysis of mutual fund holdings', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 35(3), 369-386

name: Technical analysis pays in high-volatility stocks: buy the top-volatility fifth that closes above its 20-day average, weekly (Han-Yang-Zhou)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta: universe 'US_STOCKS_WIDE' (do not also set meta.assets). Weekly rebalance. Eligible if L>=64. vol_s=sample std of ret(b,k) over k=e-62..e. Take the top 20% (round down) of eligible names by vol_s. Among them keep those with b[e].close > mean of b[k].close over k=e-19..e. Equal weight over the kept names; fewer than 3 kept -> {}.
rationale: Han, Yang and Zhou show moving-average signals earn their profits in high-volatility, high-information-uncertainty stocks, where prices adjust slowly. The rule applies the signal only inside that segment.
source: Han, Yang & Zhou 2013, 'A new anomaly: the cross-sectional profitability of technical analysis', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 48(5), 1433-1461

name: Detrended 10-year yield gate: hold equity ETFs only while the 10-year nominal yield is below its 12-month mean (Campbell; Ang-Bekaert)
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Uses cached FRED series: y(k)=ctx.macro('DFII10',k)+ctx.macro('T10YIE',k) (10-year nominal yield in percent = real yield + breakeven; return 0 if either is null). Keep a rolling window of the last 252 finite y values (ctx.rolling(252), push once per bar when finite; require full()). Return 1 iff y(i) < mean of that window; otherwise 0. Long-only, re-decided every bar.
rationale: Campbell and Ang and Bekaert find short and long rates relative to their own recent history predict equity returns negatively, so rising-yield regimes are poor for stocks. Detrending the 10-year yield is the simplest published version.
source: Campbell 1991, 'A variance decomposition for stock returns', Economic Journal 101(405), 157-179; Ang & Bekaert 2007, 'Stock return predictability: is it there?', Review of Financial Studies 20(3), 651-707

name: Earnings-season market premium: hold equity ETFs from the 15th of Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct to the 14th of the next month (Savor-Wilson)
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Let t1=bars[i].time+86400 and (m,d)=UTC month and day-of-month of t1 (the calendar day after bar i's session, which is the session the position is held over in the usual case). Return 1 iff (m in {1,4,7,10} and d>=15) OR (m in {2,5,8,11} and d<=14); otherwise 0. Long-only.
rationale: Savor and Wilson show the aggregate market earns a premium in the weeks when many firms announce earnings, as the news carries systematic risk. Peak reporting runs roughly from mid-January to mid-February and the same in each other quarter.
source: Savor & Wilson 2016, 'Earnings announcements and systematic risk', Journal of Finance 71(1), 83-138

name: Crypto price delay: long the 6 coins that react most slowly to the crypto market, weekly (Hou-Moskowitz)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta: universe 'CRYPTO_DAILY', weekly rebalance. Eligible if L>=95. m(k)=EW mean of ret(b,k) over eligible coins with bar k. Over k=e-89..e (90 obs), regress coin return r_k by OLS (with intercept) on (a) m(k) alone, giving R2_r; and (b) m(k),m(k-1),m(k-2),m(k-3),m(k-4), giving R2_u. Delay=1-R2_r/R2_u (skip coins with R2_u<=0). Long the 6 highest Delay, 1/6 each.
rationale: Hou and Moskowitz find stocks that respond to market news with a lag earn a premium for the delay (information friction). Borgards and Czudaj document large price delays in crypto, so the premium may be sizeable there.
source: Hou & Moskowitz 2005, 'Market frictions, price delay, and the cross-section of expected returns', Review of Financial Studies 18(3), 981-1020; Borgards & Czudaj 2020, Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions & Money 71, 101291

name: Chen-Roll-Ross macro exposure: long the fifth of stocks with the highest weekly beta to WTI crude oil price changes (wide US stocks)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta: universe 'US_STOCKS_WIDE' (do not also set meta.assets). Weekly rank calls. ctx.state.hist = list of {v, close:{s:b[e].close for every symbol in the view}} appended once per call (v = ctx.macro('DCOILWTICO'), latest known by the rebalance close), capped at 60 entries (drop the oldest). For symbol s, over the last 53 consecutive entries form pairs (dv_j=v_j-v_(j-1), r_j=close_j/close_(j-1)-1) where both v values are finite and s has a close in both entries; require exactly 52 pairs else skip s. beta_s=OLS slope of r on dv (plain differences of the macro level). Long the top 20% (round down) of scored names by beta_s, equal weight; fewer than 3 scored -> {}. Sign fixed a priori: the high-exposure fifth is held (exposure to a priced macro risk earns the premium). Oil level is in dollars per barrel; the weekly change is a plain dollar difference (the 2020-04-20 negative print needs no special handling).
rationale: Chen, Roll and Ross show unexpected changes in macro variables are priced risks in the cross-section of stock returns. This ranks stocks by their measured weekly exposure to WTI crude oil price and holds the most exposed fifth.
source: Chen, Roll & Ross 1986, 'Economic forces and the stock market', Journal of Business 59(3), 383-403

name: Crypto stable-volume premium: long the 6 coins with the lowest coefficient of variation of dollar volume over 90 days, weekly (Chordia-Subrahmanyam-Anshuman transfer)
rule: rank() mode; for symbol s, b=universe[s], L=b.length, e=L-1 (latest bar in the view = the rebalance-day close); ret(b,k)=b[k].close/b[k-1].close-1; windows are counted back from e; ties broken by symbol name ascending; weights >= 0 and sum <= 1, unlisted symbols = 0; fewer than the stated minimum picks -> return {} (cash that period). meta: universe 'CRYPTO_DAILY', weekly rebalance. Eligible if L>=91. dv_k=b[k].close*b[k].volume for k=e-89..e; CV_s=sample std(dv)/mean(dv) (skip if mean<=0). Long the 6 lowest CV_s, 1/6 each.
rationale: Chordia, Subrahmanyam and Anshuman find stocks with highly variable trading activity earn lower returns, so stable dollar volume marks stocks with a liquidity premium. The transfer asks whether the same ordering holds across crypto coins.
source: Chordia, Subrahmanyam & Anshuman 2001, 'Trading activity and expected stock returns', Journal of Financial Economics 59(1), 3-32

name: Noise-area intraday momentum on hourly crypto: trade breakouts of the 14-day average same-hour move around the UTC day open, flat at 23:00 (Zarattini-Barbon-Aziz)
rule: signal() mode on hourly bars, per asset; bars[0..i] only; the value at bar i is held over bar i+1. h=floor(bars[i].time/3600)%24; j0=i-h is the first (00:00 UTC) bar of the day; require bars[j0].time==bars[i].time-3600*h else return 0. open_d=bars[j0].open. For k=1..14: require i-24k>=0, j0-24k>=0, bars[i-24k].time==bars[i].time-86400k and bars[j0-24k].time==bars[j0].time-86400k else return 0; m_k=|bars[i-24k].close/bars[j0-24k].open-1| (same-hour move from that day's open). sigma=mean(m_1..m_14). Upper=open_d*(1+sigma), Lower=open_d*(1-sigma). If h==23 return 0 (flat over the day boundary). Else return +1 if close[i]>Upper, -1 if close[i]<Lower, otherwise 0 (a re-entry inside the band is automatically flat). longShort true.
rationale: Zarattini et al. show index ETF prices that leave the 'noise area' around the day's open (the average same-time absolute move) tend to keep moving until the close. Crypto has a continuous UTC day, so the same construction applies to its 24-hour cycle.
source: Zarattini, Barbon & Aziz 2024, 'Beat the market: an effective intraday momentum strategy for S&P500 ETF (SPY)', SSRN 4824172

name: Same-hour return seasonality: trade the next hour in the sign of its mean return at the same hour over the last 20 days when t>=1.5, hourly crypto (Heston-Korajczyk-Sadka transfer)
rule: signal() mode on hourly bars, per asset; bars[0..i] only; the value at bar i is held over bar i+1. Needs i>=24*20+1; require bars[i].time-bars[i-24*20].time==86400*20 else return 0. For k=1..20 let x_k=close[i+1-24k]/close[i-24k]-1 (the return of the bar covering the same hour as bar i+1 on the k-th previous day; all indices <=i-23). mean=mean(x), sd=sample std(x), t=mean/(sd/sqrt(20)) (return 0 if sd==0). Return +1 if t>=1.5, -1 if t<=-1.5, otherwise 0. longShort true.
rationale: Heston, Korajczyk and Sadka find stock returns at a given time of day correlate with returns at the same time on prior days, at lags that are exact multiples of 24 hours, which they attribute to institutional trading cycles. Crypto's hourly bars test the effect in a 24/7 market.
source: Heston, Korajczyk & Sadka 2010, 'Intraday patterns in the cross-section of stock returns', Journal of Finance 65(4), 1369-1407

name: Summer seasonal: flat 13 equity ETFs during July-September, long otherwise (Hong-Yu 'Gone fishin')
rule: signal() mode, applied independently to every listed asset (ctx.state is per asset); bars[0..i] only. A value returned at bar i is the position held over bar i+1 (close of bar i to close of bar i+1). ret(k)=bars[k].close/bars[k-1].close-1. date(k)=UTC calendar date of bars[k].time (epoch seconds; daily bars open at 00:00 UTC of the session date); dow(t)=(floor(t/86400)+4)%7 with 0=Sunday. Let m=UTC month of (bars[i].time+86400) (the calendar day after bar i's session). Return 0 if m in {7,8,9}; otherwise return 1. Long-only.
rationale: Hong and Yu find stock returns are lowest in the third quarter across many markets, when trading activity drops as investors take holidays. It is a different window from sell-in-May (May-October) and the September-only effect.
source: Hong & Yu 2009, 'Gone fishin': seasonality in trading activity and asset prices', Journal of Financial Markets 12(4), 672-702
